newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Caribbean political legend Manley dead at 72.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean political legend Manley dead at 72.

text.p: Jamaica's Michael Manley, one of the outstanding figures of modern Caribbean politics, ranged the political spectrum in four decades of leadership.
He embraced tropical socialism and flirted with Cuban President Fidel Castro, earning the wrath of the United States.
A stalwart of the Commonwealth, he hob-nobbed with Queen Elizabeth while counting reggae superstar Bob Marley among his friends.
Under his leadership, Jamaica suffered acute turmoil and political violence. But he also found time to write a definitive history of West Indian cricket.

The 40 years that saw clench-fist allegiance with Castro's socialist Cuba were eventually to include a private dinner at the White House, where President George Bush hailed him as an apostle of free-market economics.
Manley left the job of prime minister in March 1992, stepping down after a bout of pneumonia in his 40th year of involvement in Jamaican public life.

Born on December 10, 1924, Manley breathed politics from the crib. His father, Norman Manley, was a national hero who was prime minister in 1962 when Jamaica gained independence from Britain. His English-born mother, Edna, was a noted sculptor.

Manley studied at McGill University in Montreal and during World War II served as a pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force. After the war he went to the London School of Economics, where he earned an economics degree and studied under Harold Laski, one of Britain's most influential socialist theoreticians.
He returned to Jamaica in 1951 and a year later entered politics with election to the executive council of his father's People's National Party.
That year he was also named sugar supervisor of the National Workers Union, one of Jamaica's biggest unions. For the next 14 years he worked in the trade union movement and in 1962 became a senator.
Manley was elected to the Jamican House of Representatives in 1969, the same year that he succeeded his father as PNP leader, which also made him parliamentary opposition leader.

He led the party to an election victory in 1972 and became prime minister. His rhetoric turned left-wing; his official clothing became tropical casual and he ordered the party's "10 Steps to Socialism" printed in Kingston's biggest daily.
In October 1974, Manley led a roaring rally of 75,000 supporters proclaiming democratic socialism as the PNP's official ideology. Signs and placards at the gathering declared "Socialism is Love."

His socialist rhetoric -- and the hope that he might legalise marijuana -- appealed to the island's Rastafarian and reggae community, which usually shunned politics. Bob Marley played at his campaign rallies
He won a second term in 1976 in a violence-scarred election and wrapped his arms around Castro, announcing support for Cuba's airlift of troops to Angola to fight South African-backed rebel forces.
The alliance chased investors from the island in droves, drew opposition in the United States and the International Monetary Fund and led to a deep recession.
The country became deeply polarised and bloodshed occurred between supporters of the PNP and opposition leader Edward Seaga's Jamaican Labour Party, and common gangsters.

In an effort to promote national reconciliation, Marley played the One Love Peace Concert in Kingston in 1978 at which, in a remarkable scene, Manley and Seaga appeared on stage together and held hands.

The gesture failed to transform the political scene and when Manley ran for a third term in 1980, nearly 700 people died in election-related violence. Manley was defeated in a landslide by the JLP, which took 51 seats in parliament to the PNP's nine.
The transformation of Michael Manley began.
He returned to the business suit and tie of his youth and began courting the private sector, a strategy that paid off in 1989 when the PNP and its leader returned to power.
During a trip to the United States in 1990, Manley received praise and pledges of help from Bush, who said that Manley "has done a first-class job in trying to move Jamaica forward."
Before the 1989 election, Manley downplayed ideology, but said that his economic policy was aimed at social justice, equality and improvement for the poor.

His health, however, gave out and on March 28, 1992, he turned power over to P.J. Patterson, a veteran party insider who commanded the support of top business leaders and was the architect of Manley's recent economic policies.
Witty and articulate, Manley was the author of five books that displayed his wide interests, including political ideology, the Jamaican bauxite industry and West Indian cricket.
Tall, trim and fair-skinned, Manley was married four times. Three marriages ended in divorce; another wife died in 1968.
He wed for a fifth time after leaving office in 1992, marrying long-time companion Glynne Ewart at Manley's home in the hills outside of Kingston.
